_meta: A tool program name and two argument values -- one benign, one carrying an injection payload -- used to show why a harness must pass a model's tool arguments as structured parameters (an argument array or a parameterized query) rather than string-interpolating them into a command line the shell then parses. Schema validation, covered by a companion module, checks that an argument has the right type and shape: here both arguments are valid strings, so a schema check passes them both. But a schema-valid string is still just text, and if the harness builds a command by concatenating the program name and the argument into one string and hands that string to a shell, the shell re-parses it and interprets any shell metacharacters the argument contains -- so an argument like 'report.txt; delete_all data' is split by the shell's ';' into two commands, and the injected 'delete_all data' runs even though the model (or an attacker who influenced the model) only ever supplied one argument to one tool. The fix is to never build a command string from untrusted values: pass the program and its arguments as a list (argv) straight to exec with no shell, so the argument is delivered as a single opaque value and its metacharacters are inert; the equivalent for databases is a parameterized query with placeholders, where the value can never become SQL. program is the tool's program name; safe_arg is an ordinary argument; malicious_arg is a schema-valid string that hides a second command; injected_verb is the command the payload tries to smuggle in. These are the fixture; the interpolated command string, the shell's split into separate commands, the argv list, and which verbs each path executes are computed.
